function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a step‑by‑step guide you can follow locally (or in a CI environment) to accomplish everything you asked for.  
I’ll walk you through the commands, show you the files you’ll need to create/modify, and give you the exact content for each file.  
**NOTE:** I can’t actually run the commands for you, but the instructions are complete so you can execute them yourself.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
# 1.1 Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip:** If you don’t have SSH keys set up, you can clone via HTTPS instead:
> ```bash
> git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
> cd nodejs-welcome
> ```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the Repo & Create/Update Files

### 2.1 Inspect the Repo

```bash
# 2.1.1 List files
ls -R
```

Typical output (you may see something like this):

```
├── Dockerfile          # may or may not exist
├── README.md
├── package.json
├── src
│   └── index.js
├── .github
│   └── workflows
│       └── ci.yml     # may or may not exist
└── k8s
    └── deployment.yaml   # may or may not exist
```

> **What to look for:**
> * `package.json` – tells us the Node version, dependencies, and start script.
> * `src/index.js` – entry point of the app.
> * Any existing Dockerfile or Kubernetes manifests – we’ll replace or update them.

### 2.2 Create/Update Dockerfile

Create a new `Dockerfile` (or overwrite the existing one) with the following content:

```dockerfile
# 2.2.1 Dockerfile
# Use official Node LTS image as base
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set maintainer
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose port (adjust if your app uses a different port)
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command
CMD ["node", "src/index.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**
> * Uses a lightweight Alpine image.
> * Installs only production dependencies (`npm ci --only=production`).
> * Copies source after installing deps to benefit from Docker layer caching.
> * Exposes port 3000 (common for Node apps; change if your app uses another port).

### 2.3 Create Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a directory `k8s` (if it doesn’t exist) and add a file `deployment.yaml`:

```yaml
# 2.3.1 k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Adjustments:**
> * Change `image:` to point to the Docker image you’ll push (e.g., Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry, etc.).
> * Update `replicas:` if you want more or fewer pods.
> * If you need external access, change `type:` to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer`.

### 2.4 Create GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (or overwrite if it exists) with the following content:

```yaml
# 2.4.1 .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
  pull_request:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version: '18'   # match Dockerfile base

    - name: Cache npm dependencies
      uses: actions/cache@v4
      with:
        path: ~/.npm
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-node-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-node-

    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test   # assumes you have a test script

    - name: Build Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: Dockerfile
        push: false   # set to true if you want to push to a registry
        tags: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

    - name: Lint
      run: npm run lint   # optional, if you have lint script
```

> **What this workflow does:**
> * Triggers on pushes or PRs to `main`.
> * Checks out the repo, sets up Node 18, caches npm, installs deps, runs tests, builds a Docker image (but doesn’t push).
> * You can enable pushing to a registry by setting `push: true` and adding authentication secrets.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage All Changed Files

```bash
# 3.1 Stage everything
git add -A
```

> **Tip:** If you want to review what’s staged before committing:

```bash
git status
git diff --cached
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
# 4.1 Commit changes
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# 4.2 Push to remote
git push origin main
```

> **If you’re on a different branch** (e.g., `feature/docker`), replace `main` with your branch name.

---

## 🎉 Done!

You now have:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node image |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deploys the app to Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | Automates CI on pushes to `main` |

Feel free to tweak the Docker image tag, Kubernetes replica count, or CI steps to match your exact workflow. Happy coding!
